blockers.quote: He means it. So. Three problems. One, you can't spend it. Two, you can't give it. Three, you can't hand it over, because whoever holds it holds the problem, and it doubles in their pocket too.
blockers.why: No new power rule after the halfway point: transferring the doubling rule to whoever holds the money was never established.
blockers.fix: He means it. So. Three problems. One, you can't spend it. Two, you can't give it. Three, you can't hand it over, because Jonas knows it only makes the same rolls cost more.

blockers.quote: A century ago, this street ran the same race the other way. By late 1923 a loaf of bread in Berlin cost about 200 billion marks (c01). Many workers were paid twice a day, and spent their wages at once (c02).
blockers.why: Check #7, misconception first: this passage stacks a century, a year, 200 billion and twice daily. The conversion passage at line 199 repeats the overload.
blockers.fix: Replace lines 172–176 with: “Berlin once ran this race the other way. A loaf reached about two hundred billion marks (c01). Workers spent wages the moment they were paid (c02). Lotte keeps a note from that collapse above her oven. Framed. Her grandfather's.” Replace lines 199–201 with: “Lotte has watched savings change meaning overnight. When East German marks became Deutsche Marks, everything above the protected line was cut in half (c04). Lotte: Half.”

blockers.quote: Day nineteen. Two thousand six hundred. You buy a scarf. The same scarf. In case.
blockers.why: Check #6, every use has a gap: you intend to buy a duplicate and receive exactly that, so the use produces no reversal.
blockers.fix: Day nineteen. Two thousand six hundred. You buy a better scarf. It itches. You keep yours.

keep.quote: But here's the problem. Every morning you come down the stairs with yesterday's number in your head. And every morning, it's wrong.
It isn't taken from anyone. Except it is. From everyone. A little. Every night.
A coin isn't a thing. It's Lotte, agreeing to bake tomorrow.
